steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on goal-directed navigation in partially mapped environments. It should motivate why a robot needs to use non-local information (things it can't currently see) to predict unseen space, review learning-based and Learning over Subgoals approaches, and introduce our extension that swaps in a graph neural network, with the main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Problem: navigation to an unseen goal in a partial map; POMDP; need for non-local information
- Motivating example: J-Intersection environment
- Learning-driven / model-free approaches and their limits
- Learning over Subgoals (LSP): strengths and limitation
- Our contribution: LSP-GNN, graph from map skeleton, reliability, results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem setting
  - goal-directed navigation, partially-mapped environment, reach unseen goal in minimum expected time
  - modeled as POMDP; long-horizon navigation under uncertainty computationally demanding
  - many strategies learn to predict unseen space to inform behavior
  - robot must understand how non-locally available information (parts it can't currently see) informs where to go; hard for many learning-based planners
- Motivating example (Fig. 1, J-Intersection)
  - color at center of map tells whether to go left or right
  - optimal: follow hallway whose color matches the center
  - color not visible from intersection -> robot must remember what space around the corner looked like and learn how it relates to decision
  - many real-world environments need this; esp. hard at building scale
  - our aim: retain non-local knowledge, learn to use it for predictions about where to go next
- Learning-driven approaches
  - incl. model-free deep RL; shown capacity to perform well
  - no explicit map to track where it has yet to go -> unreliable, no guarantee of reaching goal
  - struggle to reason far into future -> poor performance, brittle for long-horizon planning
- LSP (Learning over Subgoals)
  - high-level abstraction for planning in partial map; state-of-the-art performance + reliability-by-design
  - actions = exploring a region of unseen space
  - fully-connected neural net estimates goodness of exploratory actions, incl. likelihood of revealing goal
  - predictions feed model-based planning -> expected cost
  - solves two problems: (1) abstraction allows learning-informed reasoning far into the future; (2) guaranteed to reach goal if a viable path exists
  - limitation: predictions use only locally observable information
- Our work
  - extend LSP (LSP-Local) by replacing learning backend with GNN (LSP-GNN)
  - uses local + non-local info to predict unseen space, complex navigation in building-scale environments
  - graph of partial map built from map skeleton to preserve topological structure
  - GNN gives accurate predictions using non-local information
  - LSP-GNN beats LSP-Local, keeps reliability guarantees (always reaches goal)
  - simulated J-Intersection, Parallel Hallway, University Building; in University Building 9.3% and 14.9% improvement over non-learned and learned baselines

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
We look at the problem of goal-directed navigation in a partially-mapped environment. Here the robot has to reach a goal it can't see in the minimum expected time. This is usually modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Long-horizon navigation under uncertainty is computationally demanding, so many strategies use learning to make predictions about the unseen space, and these predictions inform good behavior. To do well the robot has to understand how the parts of the environment it can't currently see (i.e., non-locally available information) tell it where it should go next. This is a hard problem for many existing planning strategies that rely on learning.

As a simple example, take the scenario from our J-Intersection environment in Fig. 1. The information at the center of the map, which is the color of that region, tells the robot if it should go left or right. The optimal behavior is to follow the hallway whose color is the same as the color of the center of the map. But this color is not visible from the intersection, so the robot has to remember what the space around the corner looked like and also learn how that information relates to its decision. In general many real-world environments need this kind of understanding, and it is particularly challenging in building-scale environments. In this work our aim is to let a robot keep non-local knowledge and learn to use it to make predictions about where it should go next.

Learning-driven approaches, including many model-free approaches trained with deep reinforcement learning, have recently shown that they can perform well in this domain. But when there is no explicit map that the robot can use to keep track of where it has yet to go, many of these approaches are unreliable, and there are no guarantees that they will reach the goal. Also these approaches have trouble reasoning far enough into the future to understand the impact of their actions, so they perform poorly and can be brittle and unreliable for long-horizon planning.

- LSP (Learning over Subgoals)
  - high-level abstraction for planning in partial map; state-of-the-art performance + reliability-by-design
  - actions = exploring a region of unseen space; fully-connected net estimates goodness incl. likelihood of revealing goal
  - predictions feed model-based planning -> expected cost
  - (1) reasoning far into future; (2) guaranteed to reach goal if viable path exists
  - limitation: only locally observable information
- Our work
  - LSP-Local -> LSP-GNN (GNN backend); local + non-local info; building-scale environments
  - graph from map skeleton, preserves topology; accurate predictions with non-local info
  - beats LSP-Local, keeps reliability (always reaches goal)
  - J-Intersection, Parallel Hallway, University Building; 9.3% / 14.9% over non-learned / learned baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
We look at the problem of goal-directed navigation in a partially-mapped environment. Here the robot has to reach a goal it can't see in the minimum expected time. This is usually modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Long-horizon navigation under uncertainty is computationally demanding, so many strategies use learning to make predictions about the unseen space, and these predictions inform good behavior. To do well the robot has to understand how the parts of the environment it can't currently see (i.e., non-locally available information) tell it where it should go next. This is a hard problem for many existing planning strategies that rely on learning.

As a simple example, take the scenario from our J-Intersection environment in Fig. 1. The information at the center of the map, which is the color of that region, tells the robot if it should go left or right. The optimal behavior is to follow the hallway whose color is the same as the color of the center of the map. But this color is not visible from the intersection, so the robot has to remember what the space around the corner looked like and also learn how that information relates to its decision. In general many real-world environments need this kind of understanding, and it is particularly challenging in building-scale environments. In this work our aim is to let a robot keep non-local knowledge and learn to use it to make predictions about where it should go next.

Learning-driven approaches, including many model-free approaches trained with deep reinforcement learning, have recently shown that they can perform well in this domain. But when there is no explicit map that the robot can use to keep track of where it has yet to go, many of these approaches are unreliable, and there are no guarantees that they will reach the goal. Also these approaches have trouble reasoning far enough into the future to understand the impact of their actions, so they perform poorly and can be brittle and unreliable for long-horizon planning.

The Learning over Subgoals planning approach (LSP) is a recent approach that introduces a high-level abstraction for planning in a partial map, and it gets both state-of-the-art performance and reliability-by-design. In LSP an action corresponds to exploring a particular region of unseen space. A fully-connected neural network is used to estimate how good the exploratory actions are, including the likelihood that an exploration reveals the unseen goal. These predictions are used in model-based planning to compute expected cost. LSP solves two problems: (1) its state and action abstraction lets it do learning-informed reasoning far into the future and (2) it is guaranteed to reach the goal if a viable path exists. However LSP has a limitation, which is that when it makes predictions about unseen space it only uses locally observable information, and this limits its performance.

In this paper we extend the Learning over Subgoals Planner (LSP-Local) by replacing its learning backend with a Graph Neural Network (LSP-GNN). This gives reliable learning-informed planning that can use both local and non-local information to predict unseen space, and so it improves performance in complex navigation scenarios in building-scale environments. We use a graph representation of the partial map, which is built from a map skeleton so that the topological structure is preserved, and we show that our GNN can make accurate predictions of unseen space using non-local information. We also show that our LSP-GNN planner improves performance over the original LSP-Local planner and still keeps the guarantees on reliability, i.e., the robot always reaches the goal. We show our approach works in our simulated J-Intersection, Parallel Hallway, and University Building environments. In the University Building environment it gives improvements of 9.3% and 14.9% over non-learned and learned baselines respectively.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
We focus on the task of goal-directed navigation in a partially-mapped environment, in which a robot has to reach an unseen goal in minimum expected time. Usually modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) [1], long-horizon navigation under uncertainty is computationally demanding, so many strategies turn to learning to make predictions about unseen space and thereby inform good behavior. To perform well, a robot must understand how parts of the environment it cannot currently see (i.e., non-locally available information) inform where it should go next, which is a challenging problem for many existing planning strategies that rely on learning.

Consider the simple scenario from our J-Intersection environment shown in Fig. 1: information at the center of the map (the color of that region) informs whether the robot should travel left or right; optimal behavior means following the hallway whose color matches that of the center of the map. Since this color is not visible from the intersection, a robot must remember what the space looked like around the corner to perform well and learn how that information relates to its decision. More generally, many real-world environments require this kind of understanding, which is particularly challenging for building-scale environments. In this work, we aim to allow a robot to retain non-local knowledge and learn to use it to make predictions that inform where it should travel next.

Recently, learning-driven approaches—including many model-free approaches trained via deep reinforcement learning [2,3] —have shown the capacity to perform well in this domain. However, without an explicit map the robot can use to keep track of where it has yet to go, many such approaches are unreliable and lack guarantees that they will reach the goal [4]. Moreover, these approaches struggle to reason far enough into the future to understand the impact of their actions, and so they perform poorly and can be brittle and unreliable for long-horizon planning.

The recent Learning over Subgoals planning approach (LSP) [5] introduces a high-level abstraction for planning in a partial map that allows for both state-of-the-art performance and reliability-by-design. In LSP, actions correspond to exploration of a particular region of unseen space. Learning (via a fully-connected neural network) is used to estimate the goodness of exploratory actions, including the likelihood that an exploration will reveal the unseen goal. These predictions inform model-based planning and are used to compute expected cost. LSP overcomes two problems: (1) its state and action abstraction allows for learning-informed reasoning far into the future and (2) it is guaranteed to reach the goal if there exists a viable path. However, LSP is limited: its predictions about unseen space only make use of locally observable information, which limits its performance.

In this paper, we extend the Learning over Subgoals Planner (LSP-Local), replacing its learning backend with a Graph Neural Network (LSP-GNN), which affords reliable learning-informed planning capable of using both local and non-local information to make predictions about unseen space and so improves performance in complex navigation scenarios in building-scale environments. Using a graph representation of the partial map—constructed via a map skeleton [7] to preserve topological structure—we demonstrate that our GNN allows for accurate predictions of unseen space using non-local information. We also demonstrate that our LSP-GNN planner improves performance over the original LSP-Local planner while retaining guarantees on reliability: i.e., the robot always reaches the goal. We show the effectiveness of our approach in our simulated J-Intersection, Parallel Hallway, and University Building environments, in the latter yielding improvements of 9.3% and 14.9% (respectively) over non-learned and learned baselines.
